job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I reviewed only the text you pasted, not earlier versions or the committee report. The legal cross-references below are my own reading and should go past counsel before they run in print.

**Section 2 (Definitions)**

1. **§2(1)(A), no aggregation.** The threshold applies to "a single vessel," so an operator can run several vessels (or a rotating fleet) that each stay under 10,000 tons without ever triggering the definition. Nothing treats affiliated vessels or operators as one.
2. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and "per year."** "Recovery" is undefined: it could mean collection on the seafloor, lifting to the surface, or landing ashore. "Per year" doesn't say calendar year or rolling 12 months, and tons aren't specified as wet or dry weight, which matters a lot for nodules.
3. **§2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" and "seabed."** Neither is defined, and "polymetallic nodules" isn't either. The phrase could sweep in sand and gravel dredging or even hydrocarbons, which invites an overbreadth challenge. Depending on the reading, it could also miss crusts, sulfides, or sediments.
4. **§2(1)(A), 200-meter depth.** The test applies to any seabed deeper than 200 m, including inside U.S. waters, which is broader than the "deep seabed" title suggests. It doesn't say where depth is measured on sloping terrain, and mining just shallower than 200 m is outside the definition.
5. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary" is undefined.** Nothing says which Secretary this is (Commerce, Interior, State?), and §6 uses "Secretary of State" explicitly, which makes the ambiguity worse.
6. **§2(1)(B), standard and process.** "Risks … comparable to" is vague, and there's no rulemaking, notice, deadline, or review procedure. Because §5(b) attaches criminal penalties to it, expect fair-notice, vagueness, and nondelegation challenges.
7. **§2(2), "U.S. person" gaps.** It covers only citizens and corporations organized under a *State's* law. LLCs, partnerships, trusts, permanent residents, entities organized in D.C. or territories, and foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies are all arguably outside it.
8. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** A 5,000-gross-ton floor lets a fleet of smaller vessels, barges, or seabed crawlers escape the registry entirely. "Equipped for the recovery" is also undefined and easy to contest (a ship can be reconfigured or chartered for the job).

**Section 3 (Prohibition)**

9. **§3(a), "person" and "engage in."** Neither term is defined. It's unclear whether owners, charterers, financiers, parent companies, or onshore processors "engage in" mining, which creates attribution problems.
10. **§3(a), "in the United States."** The term is undefined, so it's unclear whether it reaches the EEZ or outer continental shelf. A foreign company operating a foreign-flag vessel on the high seas is likely outside the prohibition.
11. **§3(a), no downstream controls.** The bill doesn't restrict importing, processing, purchasing, or financing minerals mined elsewhere. U.S. firms could offtake from foreign operators.
12. **§3, relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't mention the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act or OCSLA, and it doesn't amend, repeal, or preempt them. NOAA's licensing and permitting authority could therefore conflict with, or be argued to survive alongside, the prohibition. Verify against current statute.
13. **§3(b), "exploration license" is undefined.** It doesn't say the license must be U.S.-issued, so a foreign-government or International Seabed Authority contract could arguably qualify.
14. **§3(b), scope of the grandfathering.** The exemption covers "mining" (itself undefined, and different from the defined term "commercial deep seabed mining") with no volume cap, so a licensee could arguably recover commercial quantities. There's also no expiration and no limit on renewals, amendments, expansions, or transfers to new entities.
15. **§3(b), enactment-date cutoff.** A hard cutoff at enactment creates an incentive to rush license issuance or applications before the bill passes. Pending applications aren't addressed.
16. **§3(c), environmental assessment.** The exemption is purpose-based and subjective, with no volume cap, no approval or notice requirement, and no bar on selling recovered material. A company could label large-scale test mining as "assessment."

**Section 4 (Registry)**

17. **§4(a), "operator" and timing.** "Operator" is undefined (owner, charterer, manager, or shell entity?), and there's no registration deadline or lead time after the effective date.
18. **§4, no enforcement.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register or report carries no stated consequence.
19. **§4(b), report content.** "Describing the recovery activities" doesn't require tonnage, location, depth, or discharge data, and there's no due date after quarter-end. Nothing penalizes false certifications beyond whatever general law applies, and nothing addresses public disclosure versus confidential business information.
20. **§4, authority and funding.** The bill gives NOAA no rulemaking authority, no funding, and no coordination duty with the Coast Guard or DOJ. It also doesn't explain how NOAA would compel foreign-flag operators to register.

**Section 5 (Penalties)**

21. **§5(a) vs. §8, retroactivity conflict.** Civil penalties run from "the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later. Defendants will argue there is no violation before the effective date, and a retroactivity argument is possible.
22. **§5(a), no enforcement machinery.** The bill doesn't say who assesses or sues for penalties, and it has no administrative process, injunctive relief, vessel seizure or forfeiture, judicial review, or penalty factors. The absence of factors also invites Excessive Fines arguments.
23. **§5(a), daily penalty vs. annual threshold.** The offense turns on an annual tonnage threshold, but the penalty accrues "each day on which the violation occurs." It's unclear which days count, and no authority lets an agency stop an operation before it crosses the threshold.
24. **§5(b), "willfully."** It's undefined, so it's unclear whether the government must prove knowledge of the law, not just the conduct. Combined with the vague §2(1)(B), this makes prosecutions hard. There's also no separate offense for structuring operations to evade the threshold.

**Sections 6–8 (Diplomacy, Duration, Effective Date)**

25. **§6, hortatory.** "Shall seek to negotiate" requires effort, not a result. It's ambiguous whether the 18 months is a deadline to start talks or conclude an agreement. There's no reporting requirement or consequence, and "equivalent" prohibitions and the form of agreement (treaty vs. executive agreement) are unspecified.
26. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), direct contradiction.** §7(a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress makes a finding, but §7(b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless. Courts and regulated parties will read the sunset as controlling, which makes the §7(a) language misleading.
27. **§7(a), mechanism.** Nothing requires the National Academies to produce a report, sets a deadline or funding, or defines "serious harm." The legal effect of the joint resolution (repeal? suspension? conditions?) is unstated, and there's no expedited procedure. Because Congress can always change the law by statute, the clause adds little.
28. **§7(b), sunset mechanics.** There's no savings clause for pending or past violations, so defendants may argue that enforcement abates at sunset. Because the sunset runs from enactment and the Act takes effect 180 days later, the prohibition lasts only about 9.5 years. The sunset also ends the registry, and §3(b) licenses have no matching end date.
29. **§8, the 180-day gap.** Activity can begin during the window, and the bill has no transition or wind-down rule for it. That sets up vested-rights, reliance, or takings arguments against enforcement.

**General omissions**

30. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes §2(1)(B) or the criminal provision, nothing says the rest survives.
31. **No implementation provisions.** The bill has no rulemaking authority, appropriation, citizen-suit or whistleblower provision, or judicial-review language. It also lacks definitions for "Secretary," "person," "United States," and "seabed."

**Most consequential for Thursday:** items 1, 5–6, 7, 14, 16, 18, 21–22, and 26. Together they show how the prohibition could be avoided (splitting vessels, grandfathering, "assessment" labels) and why it would be hard to enforce or defend in court (retroactivity, no enforcement machinery, vagueness under criminal penalties, and the internal contradiction on duration).

I can turn this into a reader-facing explainer or a short list of questions for committee staff and stakeholders if you'd like.
